title: MSI Mystic Light RGB Software: Download, Setup, Fixes
description: MSI Mystic Light now lives inside MSI Center: install MSI Center, then add the Mystic Light module. Setup, JRGB vs ARGB headers, sync and detection fixes.
dek: Where to get MSI Mystic Light today, how to install only the part you need, which header each strip belongs on, and what to do when it will not see your lights.
quickAnswer: MSI Mystic Light is no longer a separate download on current boards. Install MSI Center from your motherboard's support page on msi.com, open its Features section and install the Mystic Light module, then restart. It controls the board's LEDs and anything on its RGB and ARGB headers. Put 12 V 4-pin strips on JRGB and 5 V 3-pin strips on the ARGB header, never the other way round.
intro: Mystic Light is MSI's lighting control for its motherboards, graphics cards and some partner parts. It started as a standalone app, moved into Dragon Center, and now sits inside MSI Center as one of several optional feature modules.

This guide covers where to download it, how to install Mystic Light without the rest of MSI Center's modules, which header each kind of strip belongs on, syncing other brands, and fixes for the common problems, including clashes with Armoury Crate, iCUE and OpenRGB. Menu wording changes between MSI Center versions, so where a label varies we describe what to look for.
stepsHeading: How to Install MSI Mystic Light, Step by Step

steps.h: Confirm your exact MSI board model
body: The model is printed on the board and shown on the BIOS main screen. In Windows, run msinfo32 and read BaseBoard Product. MSI often sells close variants, such as a WIFI and a non-WiFi version or a MAX refresh, so copy the full name before you search.

Search for your board on msi.com, open Support, then the Utility section, and download MSI Center. It is free. Get it from MSI's own site rather than a mirror: MSI suffered a ransomware breach in 2023 and has advised customers to download software and firmware only from official pages.

If Armoury Crate, iCUE, OpenRGB, SignalRGB, Gigabyte's RGB tools or an older standalone Mystic Light or Dragon Center is installed, uninstall it, or at least stop it from starting with Windows, and restart. Two programs talking to the same lighting controller cause most flicker and detection problems.

steps.h: Install MSI Center and add only the Mystic Light module
body: Run the installer and restart when asked. Open MSI Center and find the Features section, which lists optional modules. Install Mystic Light. You can skip the others if you only want lighting control; each module adds background components, and fewer modules means fewer things to go wrong.

steps.h: Set effects per device or sync them all
body: Open Mystic Light inside MSI Center. It lists the motherboard and each header or compatible device it detects. Pick a color and effect for each, or use the sync option to apply one effect to everything. To turn lighting off, choose the off or disabled effect for each device, or switch it off in the BIOS as described below.

sections.h: Is MSI Mystic Light Still a Separate App?
body: Not on current boards. MSI first shipped Mystic Light as its own program, then folded it into Dragon Center, and then replaced Dragon Center with MSI Center. Today Mystic Light is a feature module you install from inside MSI Center.

Older boards may still list a standalone Mystic Light version on their support page. Use whatever your board's page offers, and do not install the standalone app and MSI Center's module side by side, because both try to control the same lights.
MSI Center itself draws complaints in owner reports for its size and number of modules, as our [MSI review](/msi-review/) notes. Installing just Mystic Light keeps it lean.

sections.h: Where Do You Download MSI Mystic Light?
body: From msi.com. Open the support page for your motherboard or graphics card, choose the Utility section and download MSI Center. MSI also has a general MSI Center download page. After installing, add Mystic Light from the Features section.

The same support page lists BIOS files and drivers. A BIOS update sometimes includes fixes for the lighting controller, so if you are already there, check the notes. Our guide on [how to update MSI BIOS](/how-to-update-msi-bios/) covers M-FLASH and the Flash BIOS Button.

sections.h: Which MSI Header Should You Use: JRGB or ARGB?
body: Match the strip to the header every time. JRGB is a 12 V, four-pin header for standard RGB strips that show one color at a time. The addressable header is 5 V with three pins, one gap in a four-pin row, and lets each LED show its own color. MSI labels it JRAINBOW on many boards and JARGB_V2 on many newer ones.

Never plug a 5 V ARGB strip into a 12 V JRGB header. The extra voltage can burn out the LEDs at once. Check the label printed next to the header on the board and the connector on the device; if a fan or strip ships with both cable types, use the three-pin ARGB one.
Some older high-end MSI boards also have a JCORSAIR header for certain Corsair lighting products. It is not a general ARGB header; read the manual before using it.

Each header has a current limit, listed in your board's manual. A few fans or a strip or two is usually fine, but a long daisy chain can exceed it. For more devices, use a powered ARGB hub that takes its power from SATA and its signal from one board header.

sections.h: How Do You Sync Other Brands With MSI Mystic Light?
body: Anything plugged into the board's JRGB or ARGB headers syncs with Mystic Light whatever brand made it, as long as the connector and voltage match. That covers most case fans, strips and cooler pumps that use standard headers.

Mystic Light also supports some partner products directly, including certain memory kits, coolers and MSI graphics cards. Support lists change, so check MSI's Mystic Light compatibility information before buying a part for that reason.

Devices that run on their own controller, such as many Corsair, NZXT or Lian Li parts, usually need their own software. To control a mixed system from one app, SignalRGB and OpenRGB support many MSI boards. If you switch to one of them, remove the Mystic Light module so the two do not fight. For the same task on ASRock boards, see our [ASRock RGB software guide](/asrock-polychrome-rgb-software/).

sections.h: Why Is Mystic Light Not Detecting My Devices?
body: The most common cause is another lighting program holding the controller. Armoury Crate, iCUE, OpenRGB and SignalRGB can all lock it, even when running quietly in the tray. Close or uninstall them, restart, and open Mystic Light again. Windows 11's Dynamic Lighting setting can also take control of compatible devices; turn it off under Settings, Personalization, Dynamic Lighting if you want Mystic Light in charge.

Next, check the hardware. A strip on the wrong header type may show nothing or the wrong colors. Check that the arrow or 5 V mark on the plug lines up with the header's 5 V pin, and try the device on another header of the same type. Fans connected to a case hub need the hub's ARGB cable on a board ARGB header, and many hubs also need SATA power.

If the board's own LEDs are missing, check that onboard lighting is not switched off in the BIOS. Then remove the Mystic Light module, update MSI Center and reinstall the module. If it still fails, update the BIOS, which can include lighting controller fixes.

sections.h: How Do You Turn Off MSI RGB Without Software?
body: Most MSI boards have a BIOS option to switch off the onboard LEDs, and on many boards a separate option controls whether they stay lit when the PC is off or asleep. The location varies by board, so check the LED section in your manual. Once set, it works with no software installed.

That setting covers the board's own lights. Strips and fans on the headers may keep showing their own default effect. If a device ignores the BIOS setting, set it to off in Mystic Light, or check whether it runs on its own controller and needs its maker's software.

sections.h: Do You Need Mystic Light at All?
body: No. If you are happy with the default effect or want lights off, the BIOS can handle it and you can skip MSI Center entirely. Install Mystic Light if you want custom colors, synced effects across fans and strips, or control of an MSI graphics card's lighting.
If you only want an MSI card's lights off, Mystic Light through MSI Center is the official way. MSI Afterburner handles clocks and fan curves, not lighting.

mistakes: Plugging ARGB into the JRGB header
A 5 V addressable strip on the 12 V JRGB header can burn out its LEDs. Three-pin ARGB plugs go on JRAINBOW or JARGB_V2 headers; four-pin RGB plugs go on JRGB.
Running Mystic Light with Armoury Crate or iCUE
Two lighting programs fighting over one controller cause flicker, frozen colors and missing devices. Keep one program in charge and remove or disable the others.
MSI Center offers many modules you may never use. Each adds background components. Install Mystic Light alone if lighting is all you want.
Third-party copies of MSI Center or Mystic Light may be outdated or bundled with other software. Download from your product's page on msi.com.
A long chain of fans and strips can exceed a header's current rating. Use a powered ARGB hub for more than a few devices.
bottomLine: MSI Mystic Light now lives inside MSI Center. Download MSI Center from your board's support page on msi.com, remove other lighting tools, install only the Mystic Light module and restart. Put 12 V four-pin strips on JRGB and 5 V three-pin strips on the ARGB header. If devices are missing, close Armoury Crate, iCUE, OpenRGB or SignalRGB, check the header and cables, then reinstall the module or update the BIOS. To turn lights off with no software, use the BIOS.

faqs.q: Is MSI Mystic Light part of MSI Center?
faqs.a: Yes. On current boards Mystic Light is a feature module inside MSI Center. Install MSI Center from your board's support page, open the Features section and install Mystic Light.

faqs.q: Where do I download MSI Mystic Light?
faqs.a: From msi.com. Open your motherboard's support page, go to Utility and download MSI Center, then add the Mystic Light module. Older boards may list a standalone Mystic Light version instead.

faqs.q: What is the difference between JRGB and JRAINBOW on MSI boards?
faqs.a: JRGB is a 12 V four-pin header for standard RGB strips. JRAINBOW, labelled JARGB_V2 on many newer boards, is a 5 V three-pin header for addressable RGB. They are not interchangeable, and a 5 V strip on JRGB can be damaged.

faqs.q: Why is MSI Mystic Light not detecting my RGB?
faqs.a: Usually another RGB program, such as Armoury Crate, iCUE, OpenRGB or SignalRGB, is controlling the same controller. Close or uninstall it and restart. Then check the header type, the cable direction and hub power, and reinstall the Mystic Light module.

faqs.q: Can Mystic Light control Corsair or NZXT fans?
faqs.a: Only when they are plugged into the board's RGB or ARGB headers. Fans on their own controller need their maker's software, or a multi-brand tool like SignalRGB or OpenRGB.

faqs.q: Can I turn off MSI motherboard RGB without software?
faqs.a: On most MSI boards, yes. The BIOS has an option to switch off the onboard LEDs, and often a separate one for when the PC is off or asleep. Your board's manual shows where it is.

faqs.q: Do I need all of MSI Center for RGB?
faqs.a: No. Install MSI Center, then add only the Mystic Light module from its Features section. You can skip the other modules if lighting is all you want.
No. MSI Afterburner handles graphics card clocks, voltage and fan curves. Lighting on MSI cards and boards is controlled by Mystic Light inside MSI Center.
